entry: Fictional character owned by the Japanese company Sanrio. Created by Yuko Shimizu in 1974, the character first appeared on a vinyl coin purse in 1975. Sanrio depicts her as a British anthropomorphic [[Cat|white cat]] with a red bow and no visible mouth, living in a [[London]] suburb with her family. Shimizu took the name Kitty from [[Lewis Carroll]]'s *Through the Looking-Glass*. Originally marketed to pre-teenage girls, the brand found success among teenage and adult consumers from the 1990s. The brand declined in Japan after the 1990s but kept growing abroad; by 2010 the character was worth $5 billion a year, and [[The New York Times]] called her a "global marketing phenomenon." [[UNICEF]] appointed her children's ambassador, and the Japanese government named her ambassador of tourism. Sanrio theme parks based on her are in Hiji, Ōita; Tama New Town, Tokyo; and [[Shanghai]]. By 2008 there were over 50,000 branded products.

International outlaw motorcycle club whose members typically ride Harley-Davidson motorcycles. The club originated on March 17, 1948, in Fontana, California, when several small motorcycle clubs agreed to merge. With over 6,000 members and 592 charters in 66 countries, it is the largest outlaw biker club in the world. Its history includes drug trafficking and violent conflict with rival clubs, and involvement in crime has historically extended to its senior leadership. Police and intelligence agencies, including the [[United States Department of Justice]], consider it an [[Organized crime|organized crime]] syndicate.

Form of protective gear worn to protect the head. A helmet complements the [[Skull|skull]] in protecting the human brain, although ceremonial helmets without a protective function are sometimes worn, such as the policeman's helmet in the United Kingdom. Soldiers wear combat helmets, often made from [[Kevlar]] or other lightweight synthetic fibers. The word derives from *helm*, an [[Old English]] word for a protective head covering. Helmets are used in many sports, including American football, ice hockey, baseball, cricket and skiing, and in dangerous work such as [[Construction|construction]], [[Mining|mining]] and riot police duty. During the [[Middle Ages]], many military and some ceremonial helmets were developed, almost all of metal. Since the 1990s most helmets have been made from resin or plastic, which may be reinforced with fibers such as aramids.

German politician, chancellor of Germany (1982–98). He earned a doctorate in history from [[Heidelberg University]] in 1958 and led the Christian Democratic Union from 1973 to 1998. Elected chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence in 1982, he served 16 years, the longest chancellorship in German postwar history. He was committed to European integration, and with French president [[François Mitterrand]] he was an architect of the Maastricht Treaty, which established the [[European Union]] and the [[Euro|euro]] currency. Following the Revolutions of 1989, his government acted decisively, and [[German reunification]] came in 1990. He was a steadfast ally of the United States and supported [[Ronald Reagan]]'s policies to weaken the [[Soviet Union]]. He resigned as honorary CDU chairman in 2000 amid a party donations scandal that damaged his reputation at home.

Prussian field marshal and chief of staff of the Prussian Army for thirty years. He is regarded as the creator of a new, more modern method of directing armies in the field, and he pioneered the military use of railways. In 1835 Sultan [[Mahmud II]] asked him to help modernize the [[Ottoman Empire]] army, and he spent two years in [[Constantinople]], where he learned Turkish. He commanded troops in the Second Schleswig War, the [[Austro-Prussian War]] and the [[Franco-Prussian War]], and he is described as embodying "Prussian military organization and tactical genius." He is often called Moltke the Elder to distinguish him from his nephew, Helmuth von Moltke the Younger, who commanded the German army at the outbreak of World War I. He is notably the earliest-born person whose recorded voice is preserved, having made four recordings, two of which, made in October 1889, survive.

Capital and most populous city of Finland. Known in English until about 1930 by its Swedish name, Helsingfors, the city lies on the shore of the Gulf of Finland and is the seat of the Uusimaa region. About 694,000 people live in the municipality, with 1.3 million in the capital region and 1.6 million in the metropolitan area. The city is bilingual, with Finnish and Swedish as official languages, and lies 80 km north of [[Tallinn]], Estonia, 400 km east of [[Stockholm]], Sweden, and 300 km west of [[Saint Petersburg]], Russia. It is the third-largest municipality in the [[Nordic countries]], after Stockholm and [[Oslo]]. Classed as a major port city, it was rated the world's busiest passenger port in 2017. The city hosted the 1952 Summer Olympics and the 52nd [[Eurovision Song Contest]] in 2007, and was the 2012 World Design Capital.

Indian actress and politician. A leading actress of mainstream Hindi cinema, she was initially promoted as the "Dream Girl" and made her acting debut in 1963 in the Tamil film *Idhu Sathiyam*. She won the Filmfare Award for Best Actress for her dual role in *Seeta Aur Geeta* (1972) and married the actor Dharmendra in 1980. The [[Government of India]] awarded her the Padma Shri in 2000, the country's fourth-highest civilian honor. A member of the [[Bharatiya Janata Party|BJP]], she has represented Mathura in the Lok Sabha since 2014.

Common iron oxide mineral, Fe₂O₃, found in rocks and soils. It is mined as an important [[Iron|iron]] ore and is harder than pure iron but much more brittle. Its colors range from black and silver-gray to red, but all varieties leave a rust-red streak. Large deposits occur in banded iron formations, and gray hematite forms in still water or hot springs, such as those in [[Yellowstone National Park]]. The name derives from the [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] word for blood. [[Ochre]], a clay colored by hematite in amounts of 20% to 70%, is mainly used for tinting.

Branch of medicine concerned with diseases of the [[Blood|blood]]. It covers the study of the cause, prognosis, treatment and prevention of disorders affecting blood cells, platelets, clotting factors and [[Hemoglobin|hemoglobin]], as well as the bone marrow and [[Spleen|spleen]] that produce these components. Examples include [[Anemia|anemias]], bleeding and clotting disorders, and blood cancers such as [[Leukemia|leukemia]], [[Lymphoma|lymphoma]] and [[Multiple myeloma]]. Physicians who specialize in the field, called hematologists, diagnose and treat both noncancerous and cancerous disorders in hospitals and clinics, while laboratory-based hematopathologists interpret blood films and bone marrow slides. The term first appeared in the medical literature in 1743, in the work of German physician Thomas Schwenke.

Order of [[Insect|insects]] commonly called true bugs, with more than 100,000 species. Members include [[Cicada|cicadas]], [[Aphid|aphids]], planthoppers, leafhoppers, assassin bugs, [[Bed bug|bed bugs]] and shield bugs, which range from 1 mm to around 15 cm (6 in) in size. All share piercing-sucking mouthparts. Most feed on plant sap, some are bloodsucking, and others prey on insects or small invertebrates. Some species live in fresh water, such as water boatmen and giant water bugs. Hemipterans are hemimetabolous, with young [[Nymph (biology)|nymphs]] that somewhat resemble adults. Many aphids are capable of [[Parthenogenesis|parthenogenesis]], producing young from unfertilized eggs, which helps them multiply rapidly in favorable conditions. Some species are significant agricultural pests, and some kissing bugs transmit Chagas disease. A few have been cultivated for cochineal and carmine dyes and for [[Shellac|shellac]], and cicadas have been eaten as food.

Division of the globe into two equal halves. Hemispheres are typically divided into northern and southern halves by the [[Equator]], and into western and eastern halves by the [[Prime meridian]]. They can also be divided culturally, by religion, or by prominent geographic features, such as the land-water division. The Land Hemisphere, centered near 47°N, 1°E, near Nantes, France, contains the largest possible area of land, including most of the world's continents. Its counterpart, the Water Hemisphere, centered near 47°S, 179°W, in the South Pacific Ocean, contains the largest possible area of water, including most of the [[Pacific Ocean]], the Indian Ocean and the [[Southern Ocean]]. Such divisions are used to study Earth's geographic distribution, cultural differences and socioeconomic features.

[[Iron]]-containing protein that carries [[Oxygen|oxygen]] in [[Red blood cell|red blood cells]]. Almost all [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]] have hemoglobin, with the sole exception of the fish family Channichthyidae. It carries oxygen from the lungs or gills to the body's tissues, where it is released for [[Respiration (physiology)|aerobic respiration]]. In mammals hemoglobin makes up about 96% of a red blood cell's dry weight, and it can bind and transport up to four oxygen molecules. Its oxygen-binding capacity of 1.34 mL of O₂ per gram increases the total blood oxygen capacity seventy-fold compared with dissolved oxygen in plasma alone. It also carries about 20–25% of the body's respiratory [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] and the regulatory molecule [[Nitric oxide|nitric oxide]]. In 1959 Max Perutz determined its molecular structure, and he shared the 1962 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with John Kendrew. The role of hemoglobin in the blood was elucidated by the French physiologist [[Claude Bernard]].

Vascular cushions in the anal canal that help control stool. When swollen or [[Inflammation|inflamed]], they become a disease. Internal hemorrhoids often cause painless, bright red bleeding during [[Defecation|defecation]], while external ones cause pain and swelling. Constipation, [[Diarrhea|diarrhea]] and long periods on the [[Toilet|toilet]] are believed to raise abdominal pressure and contribute, and hemorrhoids are more common in [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]]. Often no treatment is needed, and symptoms frequently improve after a few days. About 50% to 66% of people have problems with hemorrhoids at some point. The first known mention is in a 1700 BC Egyptian [[Papyrus|papyrus]].

Vernacular English name for the plant *Cannabis sativa*. The plant can be refined into [[Paper|paper]], [[Rope|rope]], [[Textile|textiles]], [[Clothing|clothing]], biodegradable plastics, [[Paint|paint]], insulation, [[Biofuel|biofuel]], food and medicines. Along with [[Bamboo|bamboo]], it is among the fastest-growing plants on Earth and was one of the first plants spun into usable fiber, about 50,000 years ago. Most developed Western countries regulate the psychoactive compound tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and permit only low-THC cultivars. In many regions where hemp is a traditional crop, the distinction is not contemplated in law.

Province in central China. It is China's third-most populous province and the most populous inland one (pop., 2020: over 99 million). Its name literally means "South of the River," referring to the [[Yellow River]], and the area was historically known as the Central Plains (Zhongyuan), regarded as the core of Chinese cultural history. Four of China's historical capitals, [[Luoyang]], Anyang, Kaifeng and [[Zhengzhou]], lie within the province. The [[Shang dynasty]] (c. 1600 – c. 1046 BC) had its capitals there, and oracle bone scripts found at Yinxu in Anyang provide insight into its writing and rituals. After [[Qin Shi Huang]] unified China in 221 BC, the [[Han dynasty]] made the area Henan Commandery and made Luoyang the empire's political and cultural center. Its nominal GDP of CN¥5.88 trillion (US$926 billion) in 2021 surpassed that of Turkey.

Dutch theoretical physicist. He shared the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pieter Zeeman for their discovery and theoretical explanation of the Zeeman effect. He derived the [[Lorentz transformation]] of the [[Special relativity|special theory of relativity]], and the [[Lorentz force]], which describes the force on a charged particle in an electromagnetic field. He also developed the Lorentz oscillator model of anomalous dispersion in [[Dielectric|dielectric]] materials. In 1878 he was appointed to the newly established chair of theoretical physics at Leiden University, where he was primarily interested in electromagnetic theory, refining the ideas of [[James Clerk Maxwell|Maxwell]]. In 1912 he became curator of the Physical Cabinet at Teylers Museum in Haarlem. From 1925 until his death he chaired the International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation, the forerunner of [[UNESCO]]. He had first asked [[Albert Einstein]] to succeed him at Leiden, but Einstein declined because he had just taken a position at [[ETH Zurich]].

Vegetable [[Dye|dye]] made from the dried, powdered leaves of *Lawsonia inermis*, used for reddish stains in body art, including mehndi, or henna tattoos. It has been used since at least antiquity in the Middle East and North Africa, notably in [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]], to dye skin, hair, fingernails and fabrics such as [[Silk|silk]], [[Wool|wool]] and [[Leather|leather]]. Records show the plant was marketed in Babylonia, and it was used on some Egyptian mummies. It reached the Maghreb through Phoenician diasporas, and [[Pliny the Elder]] wrote of its use in the [[Roman Empire]] as a medicine, perfume and dye. Whole leaves do not stain the skin, because the active agent lawsone is bound within the plant; dried leaves mashed into a paste do, as lawsone migrates into the skin and binds to its proteins. The paste should stay on the skin for at least four to six hours.

French experimental physicist. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with [[Marie Curie]] and [[Pierre Curie]] for the discovery of radioactivity. After [[Wilhelm Röntgen|Röntgen]]'s discovery of [[X-ray|X-rays]] in late 1895, he looked for a link between them and the phosphorescence he had been studying. He placed [[Uranium|uranium]] salts on photographic plates wrapped in black paper, and the plates showed images even when left in a dark cabinet. He concluded that the penetrating radiation came from the uranium itself. He also identified that [[Beta particle|beta particles]] are high-speed [[Electron|electrons]], and his observations laid the groundwork for [[Ernest Rutherford]]'s theory of radioactive transmutation. He noted the physiological effects of radioactivity, which sparked its medical use in radiotherapy.

French philosopher. Bergson argued that immediate experience and intuition are more significant than abstract [[Rationalism|rationalism]] and science for understanding reality, and his influence in [[Analytic philosophy|analytic]] and continental philosophy was strongest in the first half of the 20th century. His four principal works were *Time and Free Will* (1889), *Matter and Memory* (1896), *Creative Evolution* (1907) and *The Two Sources of Morality and Religion* (1932). From 1900 to 1904 he held the chair of Greek and Roman philosophy at the Collège de France, and then the chair of modern philosophy until 1920. He received the 1927 Nobel Prize in Literature "in recognition of his rich and vitalizing ideas," and in 1930 France gave him its highest honor, the Grand-Croix of the Légion d'honneur. His popularity provoked controversy, as his views were seen as opposing the "secular and scientific" attitude of the Republic's officials.

French humanist photographer and artist. Considered a master of candid photography and an early user of 35mm film, he pioneered street photography. He viewed capturing the "decisive moment" as the essence of the very best pictures. He studied painting under the Cubist André Lhote in [[Paris]], whose aim was to link the French classical tradition to [[Modernism|modernism]]; he later regarded Lhote as his teacher of "photography without a camera." In the 1920s he socialized with the [[Surrealism|Surrealists]], and the movement's founding in 1924 was a catalyst for a paradigm shift in photography. He was one of the founding members of Magnum Photos in 1947. In the 1970s he largely discontinued photography to paint.

French painter, draftsman, printmaker and sculptor. Along with [[Pablo Picasso]], he is commonly regarded as one of the artists who best helped define the revolutionary developments in the visual arts during the opening decades of the 20th century. The intensity of his colors from 1900 to 1905 brought him notoriety as one of the Fauves (French for "wild beasts"). After 1906 he developed a rigorous style that emphasized flattened forms and decorative pattern. In 1917 he moved to a suburb of [[Nice]] on the French Riviera, and the more relaxed style of his 1920s work earned acclaim as an upholder of the classical tradition in French painting. After 1930 he adopted a bolder simplification of form. In 1896 he visited the Australian painter John Russell on Belle Île, off the coast of [[Brittany]], who introduced him to [[Impressionism]] and to the work of [[Vincent van Gogh]]. When ill health prevented him from painting in his final years, he created an important body of work in [[Collage|cut-paper collage]].

French mathematician, theoretical physicist, engineer and philosopher of science. Often described as a polymath, he is called "The Last Universalist" in mathematics, having excelled in every field of the discipline as it existed in his lifetime. In his research on the [[Three-body problem|three-body problem]], he became the first to discover a chaotic deterministic system, laying foundations of modern [[Chaos theory|chaos theory]]. He is regarded as the creator of [[Algebraic topology|algebraic topology]], and early in the 20th century he formulated the [[Poincaré conjecture]], which was solved in 2002–2003 by Grigori Perelman. He was the first to present the [[Lorentz transformation|Lorentz transformations]] in their modern symmetrical form, and he helped lay the foundations of [[Special relativity|special relativity]]. In a 1905 letter to [[Hendrik Lorentz]] he recorded the remaining relativistic velocity transformations. Philosopher [[Karl Popper]] regarded him as the greatest philosopher of science of all time. He served as president of the French Academy of Sciences in 1906.

French post-Impressionist painter in the naive or primitive manner. Known as Le Douanier (the customs officer), a humorous description of his job as a toll and tax collector in Paris, he began painting seriously in his early forties and retired from his job at 49 to paint full-time. Critics ridiculed him during his lifetime, but he came to be recognized as a self-taught artist of high quality. Although he rarely traveled, he painted [[Jungle|jungle]] scenes based on plants and animals he saw in Paris's natural history museum and botanical garden. His painting *The Hungry Lion Throws Itself on the Antelope* was exhibited in 1905 near works by [[Henri Matisse]] and other younger avant-garde artists, in what is seen as the first showing of the Fauves. In 1908 [[Pablo Picasso]] held a banquet in his studio in honor of Rousseau, now considered one of the most notable social events of the twentieth century. His work influenced several generations of [[Avant-garde|avant-garde]] artists.

French painter, printmaker, draftsman, caricaturist and illustrator. Born into an aristocratic family, he broke both legs as an adolescent, and his legs stopped growing at about 1.52 m (5 ft 0 in), leaving him with an adult torso. His parents were first cousins, and his congenital conditions have often been attributed to [[Inbreeding|inbreeding]]. He returned to Paris in 1882 to study painting and settled in Montmartre, an area he rarely left for the next 20 years. Later he developed an affinity for [[Brothel|brothels]] and prostitutes, which shaped the subjects of many works recording bohemian life in late 19th-century Paris. He is among the Post-Impressionists, with [[Paul Cézanne]], [[Vincent van Gogh]], [[Paul Gauguin]] and [[Georges Seurat]] also commonly considered part of the loose group.

African-American woman whose cervical [[Cancer|cancer]] cells were the source of the HeLa cell line. Cells from a tumor biopsied at Johns Hopkins Hospital in [[Baltimore]], Maryland, in 1951 were cultured by George Otto Gey, creating the first immortalized human cell line. As was then the practice, no [[Consent|consent]] was required, and the Lacks family was not made aware of the line until 1975. HeLa cells are still used in medical research, and the case continues to raise concerns about [[Privacy|privacy]] and patients' rights.
